clue.text: Weirdo Sid Owen tackles a bit of a dance

indicators.note: to tackle is to grip, so the phrase holds the answer's letters

parts.note: weirDO SID Owen: the answer runs across the word breaks

explanation.surface: An odd character called Sid Owen is attempting a dance step.
explanation.walkthrough: Sid Owen is a real actor, so the name reads as the subject; it is only the container for the letters. 'Tackles' looks like football, not a hidden-word signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A do-si-do is a figure in square dancing where partners circle back to back, so it is one bit of a dance.

clue.text: Stop son being adopted by believer in God

parts.note: a deist believes in God without revealed religion

explanation.surface: A son is taken in by a devout family, and someone wants it stopped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Adopted' paints a family scene; it is the container signal, taking S into the believer. A deist believes in a creator God but not in revelation.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: to desist is to cease, used of an action one is told to give up.

clue.text: Cry before party managed to clear one's head

explanation.surface: Someone weeps before a party and somehow gets their thoughts straight.
explanation.walkthrough: The DUP is the Democratic Unionist Party of Northern Ireland. The picture of tears before a party hides a morning-after answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Having sobered up, one's head is clear again after drinking.

clue.text: Band member Joe famously losing stone for daughter

indicators.note: to lose something is to go without it, so ST drops out of the name
'for' in the sense of 'in exchange for'

parts.note: Joe STRUMMER without ST (stone, the weight)

explanation.surface: A famous rocker called Joe is dropping weight, apparently for his daughter's sake.
explanation.walkthrough: Joe Strummer was the singer of The Clash, so 'Band member' feels like it belongs to the wordplay. ST is the standard abbreviation for stone, the 14-pound weight.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by role: the drummer keeps the beat in a band, and the surface's rock star makes it apt.

clue.text: Cold Bud also served — a gassy drink lacking flavour

indicators.note: the letters are dished up in a new arrangement

parts.note: standard abbreviation, as on a tap

explanation.surface: A bar order: a cold Budweiser, plus something fizzy and bland.
explanation.walkthrough: Bud is Budweiser beer, which makes the whole thing read as a drinks order; the brand name is just letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Club soda is carbonated water, fizzy and without flavour.

clue.text: Is it Victor's round?

parts.note: read as a man called Victor, and meant as the victor, whoever has just won
read as his turn to buy the drinks, and meant as a circuit of the track

explanation.surface: Someone in a pub asks whether it is Victor's turn to buy the drinks.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital V hides the plain word victor, and the pub setting makes 'round' a round of drinks rather than a lap.
explanation.definitionFit: A lap of honour is the celebratory circuit a race winner runs, so it is literally the victor's round.

clue.text: Swaggering display from Charlie's predecessor screening commercial

indicators.note: to screen is to hide behind

parts.note: in the NATO alphabet Alpha, Bravo, Charlie: Bravo comes before Charlie

explanation.surface: A showy performance from the man who had Charlie's job before, blocking an advert.
explanation.walkthrough: Charlie looks like a person with a predecessor in office; it is a letter of the radio alphabet, and the one before it is Bravo.
explanation.definitionFit: Bravado is a bold, swaggering show of confidence.

clue.text: Due over £1000 after securing victory

indicators.note: 'after' in its sense of 'following'
to secure is to hold fast

parts.note: O = over, as on a cricket scorecard

explanation.surface: A payment of over a thousand pounds falls due after someone wins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Over' reads as 'more than' the sum; it is simply O. A grand is slang for £1000.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: money that is due is still owing to someone.

clue.text: Lawyer dined outside, in two minds over starter of yakitori

indicators.note: a starter is what comes first, so take the first letter

explanation.surface: A lawyer eats outdoors, dithering over a skewer of Japanese chicken for a starter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dined outside' paints eating al fresco; 'outside' is the container signal. Yakitori is Japanese grilled chicken on skewers.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym with a regional lean: attorney is the usual American word for a lawyer.

clue.text: Quiet vehicle on the way back departs Uxbridge empty

indicators.note: an empty word has lost its contents, leaving only its outer letters

explanation.surface: A quiet bus on its return journey leaves Uxbridge with no passengers.
explanation.walkthrough: Uxbridge is a town on the western edge of London, which suits the bus picture. 'Quiet' is a verb here, not an adjective describing the bus.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym, as verbs: to quiet a rowdy crowd is to subdue it.

clue.text: One likely to experience a buzz at work?

definitions.text: One likely to experience a buzz at work?

parts.note: read as feeling a thrill, and meant as hearing bees hum
the job itself is where the humming happens: tending hives

explanation.surface: Someone who gets a thrill from their job.
explanation.walkthrough: A buzz reads as excitement; for a beekeeper it is the noise of the hives.
explanation.definitionFit: An apiarist keeps bees, so their working day is spent amid buzzing.

clue.text: Specialist at Rugby School initially caught harmful flies

indicators.note: the letters fly about into a new order
take the first letter of School

parts.note: C = caught, on a cricket scorecard

explanation.surface: At Rugby School, someone has caught dangerous insects.
explanation.walkthrough: Rugby School is a famous English boarding school, and the capital S makes it one phrase; split it so 'Rugby' goes with the definition and 'School' with the wordplay. 'Flies' looks like insects.
explanation.definitionFit: The scrum half is a specialist rugby position, feeding the ball into the scrum.

clue.text: Each April, go around the Aegean

definitions.note: a definition by example: the Aegean islands are the original archipelago

indicators.note: the letters are moved around

explanation.surface: An invitation to tour the Greek islands every spring.
explanation.walkthrough: The word archipelago was first the name of the Aegean Sea itself, with its scattering of islands, so the definition is historically exact.
explanation.definitionFit: The Aegean, dotted with islands, is the original archipelago.

clue.text: Carnegie regularly displayed onset of real temper

indicators.note: what is displayed at regular intervals is every other letter
the onset of something is its beginning, so take the first letter

explanation.surface: Andrew Carnegie routinely showed the first signs of a genuine temper.
explanation.walkthrough: Andrew Carnegie was the steel magnate, a plausible subject for a temper; his name here only supplies alternate letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: temper in the sense of a fit of rage, as in 'lose one's temper'.

clue.text: Cathedral cook toyed with a bit of Black Magic

indicators.note: the letters are played with into a new order

explanation.surface: A cook at a cathedral dabbled in the occult.
explanation.walkthrough: Black Magic is a British box of dark chocolates; the capitals are the only hint that it is a brand, not sorcery.
explanation.definitionFit: Each piece in a box of Black Magic is a dark chocolate.

clue.text: Like a tumbler going from bar to bar?

definitions.text: Like a tumbler going from bar to bar?

parts.note: read as a drinking glass, and meant as a gymnast who tumbles
read as a pub crawl, and meant as swinging between trapeze bars

explanation.surface: A glass being passed along from pub to pub.
explanation.walkthrough: The drinking reading of both 'tumbler' and 'bar' is so natural that the circus reading is easy to miss.
explanation.definitionFit: A tumbler flying from bar to bar is performing acrobatics.

clue.text: Fuel smell upset airborne soldier at the front

indicators.note: to upset is to knock over

parts.note: niff is British slang for a bad smell

explanation.surface: A whiff of fuel bothers the paratrooper leading the way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upset' looks like the soldier being bothered by the smell; it is the turnaround signal. Niff is British slang for a stink.
explanation.definitionFit: Paraffin is a fuel, what Americans call kerosene.

clue.text: Whisk a red pepper with oil for the perfect look

indicators.note: whisking mixes the letters up

explanation.surface: A cooking tip: blend red pepper with oil to make a dish look just right.
explanation.walkthrough: The kitchen surface makes 'Whisk' an instruction to the cook. Apple-pie order has nothing to do with pie: it means everything neat.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: apple-pie order means perfect neatness, so a room in it has the perfect look.

clue.text: Overshadow cuts in electronic energy

explanation.surface: A blackout of electrical power casts a shadow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cuts in electronic energy' reads as power cuts; 'cuts' is a verb and 'in' the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym by metaphor: one body eclipsing another blocks its light, just as a rival overshadows.

clue.text: Desperate character rues playing a bloke in tights

indicators.note: the letters of RUES perform in a new arrangement

parts.note: Desperate Dan, the cowboy strongman of the British comic The Dandy

explanation.surface: A man in despair regrets taking on the role of someone in tights.
explanation.walkthrough: Desperate Dan is the pie-eating giant of the British children's comic The Dandy, so 'Desperate character' is a named figure, not a mood.
explanation.definitionFit: A danseur is a male ballet dancer, and ballet men dance in tights.

clue.text: Stuck in Agadir by hotel, flipping cross

indicators.note: the answer is lodged inside the phrase
the letters are turned the other way

explanation.surface: Someone stranded in Agadir next to their hotel is furious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' reads as a mild curse, flipping cross meaning very angry; it is the reversal signal, and 'cross' is a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: A hybrid is a cross between two breeds or varieties.

clue.text: Associated Press: China Shock

parts.note: china plate = mate in Cockney rhyming slang, and a mate is a pal

explanation.surface: A news-agency headline about a shock in China.
explanation.walkthrough: China is the country in the headline; in Cockney rhyming slang 'china plate' means mate, shortened to china.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym, as verbs: to appal is to horrify or shock.

clue.text: Vertical chimney oil company put up outside

parts.note: lum is the Scots word for a chimney

explanation.surface: An oil company erects a tall chimney outdoors.
explanation.walkthrough: Lum is Scots for chimney, a crossword regular; 'put up' sounds like building, but it flips BP upward.
explanation.definitionFit: Plumb means exactly vertical, as a plumb line hangs.

clue.text: He's sent to fetch injured Red Baron back from Blighty

indicators.note: injured letters are damaged out of shape, so rearrange them
the back of a word is its end, so take the last letter

explanation.surface: An airman is sent to bring the wounded Red Baron home from Britain.
explanation.walkthrough: The Red Baron was the German First World War flying ace, and Blighty is old soldiers' slang for Britain, so the surface is a wartime story. 'Back from' means the last letter, not a return trip.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by role: fetching and carrying is exactly the errand boy's job.

clue.text: Murder of rejected university student drama

indicators.note: turned back, so OF becomes FO

explanation.surface: A student play about a murder was turned down by the university.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rejected university student' reads as one unlucky applicant; 'rejected' only turns back the little word 'of'.
explanation.definitionFit: Police suspecting foul play suspect murder.

clue.text: Metal safe storing whiskey

parts.note: peter is old criminal slang for a safe

explanation.surface: A metal safe with a bottle of whiskey locked inside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Metal safe' reads as one object; 'Metal' is the definition, and peter is safecrackers' slang for a safe.
explanation.definitionFit: Pewter is a tin-based metal alloy.

clue.text: Swiss bar closing early to switch walls, getting a kind of mould

indicators.note: the word stops before its last letter
the outside letters change places

parts.note: TOBLERONE, the Swiss chocolate bar, minus its last letter
the outer letters T and N swap places

explanation.surface: A Swiss bar shuts early to change its décor, and mould turns up.
explanation.walkthrough: The Swiss bar is Toblerone, the triangular chocolate, not a place to drink; its 'walls' are its first and last letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Noble rot is the grey mould Botrytis, prized for shrivelling grapes into sweet wine.

clue.text: Ready for attack, Pitt taking on both Conservative wings

indicators.note: a word's wings are its outer letters, as a party's wings are its extremes
both wings, left and right, not just one

explanation.surface: Prime Minister Pitt takes on both factions of the Tory party.
explanation.walkthrough: Pitt with Conservative reads as William Pitt, the Tory Prime Minister; it is Brad Pitt the film star.
explanation.definitionFit: Braced means prepared for an impact or attack.
